name: National QC Strategy Critique
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Grading a National Strategy: The Government as Portfolio Manager
lesson.summary: A national quantum strategy is, whether it says so or not, a portfolio allocation decision made with public money on a political clock, and it can be graded with the same diversification and uncertainty tools used on a private investor's portfolio.
lesson.body:
Government funding pressure already established that public quantum programs run on a political clock, appropriated in cycles, reviewed by legislators, vulnerable to budget cuts if progress looks slow relative to cost. This chapter adds the other half of the picture: a national quantum strategy is also a portfolio, spread across fault-tolerant computing research, quantum sensing, workforce training, and cryptographic migration, and it can be evaluated with the identical diversification and uncertainty type tools used on a private investor's holdings, just at a much larger scale and with a different set of pressures shaping the numbers.

Picture a hypothetical national strategy document, a composite built from the pattern real programs tend to follow rather than any specific country's actual budget. It allocates the large majority of its funding to fault-tolerant quantum computing research, framed around a specific milestone year, a smaller share to quantum sensing and communications, and a modest workforce training line, with almost nothing allocated to accelerating the migration of critical infrastructure to post-quantum cryptography. Applying portfolio allocation analysis to this mix surfaces the first problem immediately: the strategy is heavily concentrated in the deep uncertainty end of the required breakthroughs, the fault-tolerant computing bet depends on the same unresolved algorithmic and error correction questions private investors were warned to size cautiously, and the document does not explain why that concentration is the right national bet rather than a more diversified one.

Applying risk-adjusted returns thinking sharpens the critique further. Quantum sensing already generates revenue and rests on solved physics, meaning public money spent there buys a more certain, if smaller, payoff, faster domestic manufacturing capability, defense and infrastructure applications that work today. Fault-tolerant computing research buys a much larger potential payoff attached to a much less certain timeline. A strategy that funds only the second and starves the first is making a concentrated bet on the more extraordinary claim, which is a defensible choice for a portion of a national research budget, but an indefensible choice for nearly all of it, for exactly the reason a single investor should not put an entire portfolio into the correlated, deep uncertainty end of the spectrum.

The honesty test from each breakthrough is uncertain is worth applying directly to the document's own language. Does the strategy distinguish, anywhere in its text, between the breakthroughs it is funding that are closer to engineering problems, likely to yield to the sustained investment it is proposing, and the ones that depend on open scientific questions that money alone cannot guarantee solving on the stated timeline. A strategy that promises a specific capability by a specific year without that distinction is reclassifying deep uncertainty as a scheduling problem, the same move red flags in tech claims warned against, just written at government scale and backed by a budget request instead of a stock pitch.

None of this means government funding of ambitious, long horizon quantum research is a mistake. The earlier chapter on funding pressure was explicit that public capital has historically supported basic research private markets would have underfunded on their own, precisely because private investors need nearer term returns that early stage science cannot promise. The critique here is narrower and more useful than a broad case for or against public funding: a well built national strategy should look diversified across certain and uncertain bets the way a well built investment portfolio does, should state honestly which of its promised breakthroughs are engineering problems and which are open scientific questions, and should be judged, cycle over cycle, against the predictions it actually made rather than against how much progress it claims in hindsight. A legislator, a journalist, or a citizen asking whether a national quantum strategy deserves its budget is really asking the same portfolio question an investor asks about a fund, just with a different set of stakeholders owed the answer.
